answers.text: Tell the assistant: always return exactly three lines - delivery date, item and quantity, and any change from the original order - in that order, using the same labels each time, like 'Date:', 'Item:', 'Change:', so each line always means the same thing.
Ask the assistant to list each claim on its own line - date, amount, category, submitter - then add up the amount column for a total at the bottom of the memo.
The date in the email doesn't add up - it says three days out but the call it's referring to was earlier than that.
62 up from 54 checks out as about 15%. But 3 late out of 62 works out closer to 95%, not the 97% the report gives.

I'd sign off Output 2 - it shows the €612,000 and €25,100 behind the 4.1%, so anyone can redo the sum. Output 1 could well be correct too, but there's no way to check it without re-running the query yourself.
Reply 2, because it names the order number and the credit reference. Reply 1 says 'entirely our error' but gives nothing you could actually look up to confirm that.
1. No. 2. Yes. 3. No, better to hold off. 4. Yes. 5. No.
The pricing and discount terms are sensitive, so I wouldn't paste those in as they are. The confidentiality clause naming both companies makes me cautious about the whole thing too.
Before I send the weekly report out, I cross-check the headline numbers against the source system rather than just reading it over.

Step 4, sending the confirmation automatically, is the one that most needs a check, because once it's sent there's no taking it back. Step 1, reading the order, matters too since a wrong read carries through everything after it.
